item.title: Devitrification: crystal nucleation and growth mechanisms in glasses
item.description: arXiv:2611.08667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: If a liquid is cooled rapidly, it may fall out of equilibrium before it can crystallize. It may, however, crystallize later from the nonequilibrium glassy state. Using the Random First-Order Transition (RFOT) theory of glasses, we discuss a variety of mechanisms of crystallization as a route to devitrification. Ordinary nucleation is sped up by the frozen in energy of the glass relative to the liquid. At sufficiently low temperatures, a mechanism of nanonucleation appears, producing nanometer scale crystal inclusions in the glass. Nanocrystallization depends strongly on the local fluctuations in stability, and the transition from classical nucleation and growth to nanocrystallization occurs dominantly through rare, less stable glassy regions that percolate through space, producing an additional dramatic speedup in the crystal nucleation and growth rates. Similar fluctuations in local stability also explain anomalies of crystal growth in deeply supercooled systems.
item.dc:creator: Max Brown, Peter Wolynes

item.title: Evaporation-induced colloidal diffusiophoresis in electrolyte solutions
item.description: arXiv:2611.08965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-volatile solutes accumulate near a receding drying front, generating concentration gradients that can drive directional colloidal transport by diffusiophoresis. This dynamic spatial arrangement of colloidal particles could affect the microstructure and macroscopic properties of the dried film. Here, we combine experiments and theory to investigate polystyrene particles suspended in electrolyte solutions drying within a capillary tube. By varying the electrolyte composition and ambient relative humidity, we show that evaporation-induced ion gradients drive particles toward the liquid-gas interface and enhance interfacial accumulation, whereas slower drying at higher humidity weakens the gradient and particle migration. We use the heat balance integral method to predict the transient solute field for a receding interface and couple it to particle transport to capture the observed particle trajectories and accumulation trends. These results identify background electrolytes and drying rate as coupled controls on particle distribution and provide a predictive framework to optimize formulation and processing parameters for manufacturing slurry-based materials, such as battery electrodes and turbine coatings.
item.dc:creator: Dang Q. Duong, Jung Hyun Kim, Hanna Cho, Sangwoo Shin

item.title: Influenza A Virus as a Multivalent Active Particle: Statistical Mechanics of Binding, Motility, and Antiviral Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.09696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this contribution, we review existing multivalent models of Influenza A Virus (IAV) systems to study virion dynamics and design of multivalent entry blockers. We review existing biochemical estimations of the dissociation constants and catalytic activities of the two virion ligands [hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA)], which can be used to develop quantitative theories and experiments. Multivalent models are statistical mechanics frameworks for studying the simultaneous interaction of multiple reversible ligand-receptor bonds. They quantify the effects of both combinatorial entropy terms and single-molecule ligand-receptor affinities. Multivalent frameworks led to the rationale of superselectivity, the ability of probes to sense specific concentrations of conjugated receptors. Multivalent models guided the design of antiviral nanomedicines constituted by polymeric scaffolds conjugated with small molecules such as sialic acid receptors targeting the ligands on the surface of the virion. Importantly, neuraminidase is an enzyme that limits the number of host-guest bonds through receptor desialylation. Like active particles, neuraminidase activity enhances virion motility in the extracellular medium. Modeling the dynamics of Influenza A virions requires developing out-of-equilibrium multivalent models.
item.dc:creator: Sumati Bhatia, Andreas Herrmann, Thomas Kolbe, Lalan Kumar, Daniel Lauster, Susanne Liese, Bortolo Matteo Mognetti

item.title: Reversible Interchain Associations Dominate Plateau Elasticity in Conjugated Polymers
item.description: arXiv:2611.09810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The modulus plateau is widely regarded as a hallmark of topological entanglement in homopolymer melts and has been used to identify entanglement in semiflexible conjugated polymers. Using regiorandom poly(3-alkylthiophenes) as a model system, we show that their plateau elasticity relaxes through an Arrhenius process decoupled from segmental and terminal dynamics, reorganizes persistently under mechanical perturbation, and varies systematically with side-chain length. These behaviors are hard to reconcile with a purely topological-entanglement picture and instead support a transient network dominated by reversible interchain associations, consistent with {\pi}-{\pi} interactions between conjugated backbone segments. The results thus demonstrate that plateau elasticity alone does not uniquely identify topological entanglement in conjugated polymers. More broadly, they identify the strength and lifetime of interchain association as molecular design parameters linking backbone packing to stress relaxation, viscoelastic properties, and processability in conjugated polymers, complementing their established role in electronic structure and charge transport.
item.dc:creator: Juncheng Zheng, Xiaobing Zuo, Xiaodan Gu, Shiwang Cheng

item.title: Electrohydrodynamic interactions of two Quincke rotors: asymptotic theory and boundary element simulations
item.description: arXiv:2611.08807v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Weakly conducting spheres suspended in a leaky dielectric fluid can undergo spontaneous Quincke rotation when the applied electric field exceeds a critical value. We investigate how electric and hydrodynamic interactions modify this instability and the subsequent rotation of two spheres at fixed separation and orientation. Starting from electric dipole and hydrodynamic rotlet interactions, we develop a systematic far-field asymptotic theory. Away from onset, slow drift of the rotation axes makes a regular expansion fail at long times. A multiple-scale expansion gives slow phase equations that select the axes according to pair orientation and field strength. Near onset, weak interactions produce corrections comparable to the isolated rotation magnitude. A detuned multiple-scale expansion gives coupled equations for the transverse dipole amplitudes. Their linearization identifies four collective rotation modes, whose critical fields and steady branches with one active mode are determined together with their stability. At leading order near onset, electric interaction shifts all four modal thresholds equally, whereas hydrodynamic interaction makes counter-rotation appear first for pair angles below $\cos^{-1}(1/\sqrt3)\simeq54.7^\circ$ and co-rotation above it. Away from onset, the angle separating stable counter-rotation from stable co-rotation increases with field strength. Boundary element method (BEM) simulations place onset within a field interval for each configuration and resolve the growth and relaxation of rotation. Steady-speed comparisons show how pair orientation changes the balance between electric and hydrodynamic effects. We compare the unexpanded dipole-rotlet model of Das and Saintillan [Phys. Rev. E 87, 043014 (2013)] with our asymptotic theory and BEM simulations.
item.dc:creator: Debasish Das

item.title: Conformationally frustrated epitaxy at heteromolecular interface
item.description: arXiv:2611.08851v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Precise control of molecular heteroepitaxy offers a route to multilayer architectures with well-defined interfaces. However, the role of intramolecular flexibility in epitaxial matching remains insufficiently understood. Here, we investigate the heteroepitaxy of intact 1,3,5-tris(4-carboxyphenyl)benzene (BTB) on a molecular $\delta$-layer composed of fully deprotonated BTB molecules on Ag(111). Combining scanning tunneling microscopy, low-energy electron microscopy and diffraction, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and density functional theory, we identify the key interactions controlling molecular packing and epitaxial growth. We show that intermolecular bonding motifs are preserved on the molecular template, but their lattice parameters and molecular conformations change as compared to a silver surface. Individual molecules exhibit distinct appearances in scanning tunneling microscopy, consistent with site-dependent conformational variations identified by theory. Our calculations reveal that the competition between molecule-substrate interactions and conformational energy produces different compromise geometries, resulting in conformational frustration at the epitaxial interface. Crucially, constraining BTB into a planar geometry changes the preferred lateral adsorption positions, demonstrating that molecular flexibility directly modifies the energetic preferences for epitaxial registry. Comparison with more rigid molecular overlayers further supports this interpretation. Our findings reveal that molecular flexibility contributes to epitaxial matching by allowing unfavorable molecule-substrate interactions to be compensated by energetically favorable conformations while preserving the intermolecular network.
item.dc:creator: Jakub Planer, Pavel Proch\'azka, Tom\'a\v{s} Kraj\v{n}\'ak, Veronika Star\'a, Daniela Hrub\'a, Zden\v{e}k Endstrasser, Tom\'a\v{s} Sk\'ala, Jan \v{C}echal

item.title: Increased Crystal Nucleation in the Glassy State of a Polymer/Water Mixture
item.description: arXiv:2611.09456v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Within classical nucleation theory, crystal nucleation requires sufficient supersaturation, but is suppressed at low temperatures due to reduced molecular mobility, leading to a maximum nucleation rate typically above the glass transition temperature $T_g$. Here, we experimentally show that this conventional picture breaks down in a biocompatible polymer poly(2-methoxyethyl acrylate)(PMEA)/water mixture. We find that the number of nuclei increases dramatically below $T_g$, with the effective nucleation rate exhibiting an unusual maximum at approximately $T_g-10$ K. Calorimetric experiments reveal a strong temperature-history dependence of cold crystallization of water in hydrated PMEA, which is explained by the observed nucleation behavior. We propose that the unusual enhancement of nucleation below $T_g$ provides a key mechanism linking high glass-forming ability and cold crystallization upon heating, thereby explaining the striking asymmetry in crystallization behavior between cooling and heating. Our findings suggest that a hidden nucleation-rate maximum below $T_g$ may also underlie cold crystallization in other glass-forming liquids.
item.dc:creator: Mika Kobayashi, Shingo Kobayashi, Kazuyoshi Shiga, Hiroaki Yamada, Masaru Tanaka

item.title: Numerical investigation of the equilibrium Kauzmann transition in a two-dimensional atomistic glass
item.description: arXiv:2507.03590v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dense liquids gradually transform into non-equilibrium amorphous solids as they pass through the experimental glass transition. Experimentally, ergodicity is lost because measurements are conducted within a finite time window. More than seventy years ago, Kauzmann posed a fundamental question: If experiments could run indefinitely, would there exist a critical temperature at which an ergodicity-breaking phase transition occurs? Random first-order transitions represent the modern theoretical framework for this idea. However, theoretical calculations in finite dimensions are challenging, whereas experimental and numerical limitations on accessible timescales hinder direct observation of the putative Kauzmann transition. Here, we overcome this longstanding barrier by developing a computational strategy that properly combines three Monte Carlo methods to access the desired equilibrium thermodynamic properties of a two-dimensional atomistic glass-former down to zero temperature across a range of system sizes up to 77 particles. This enables us to directly measure thermodynamic and structural observables that provide unambiguous evidence that the system undergoes a finite-size version of the Kauzmann transition at a temperature that is much lower than other energy scales and decreases rapidly with system size, thus suggesting the existence of a zero-temperature Kauzmann transition for two-dimensional glasses. The transition is towards an ideal glass state characterized by a complex energy landscape and a hierarchical organization of low-lying states.

item.title: Broadband molecular dynamics simulation of confined Brownian motion
item.description: arXiv:2606.24291v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Molecular dynamics with an explicit solvent resolves the hydrodynamic response of a Brownian colloid in bulk and near a rigid wall over acoustic, inertial, and diffusive time scales. Bulk spectra establish a continuum reference and reveal departures associated with discrete-solvent dynamics. Under confinement, thermal spectra provide a measurement of the space-dependent added mass, while velocity autocorrelations determine space-dependent, anisotropic hydrodynamic memory and diffusion. All together, these measurements connect the enhanced added mass and reduced mobility near a wall, and probe the discrete-continuum crossover.
item.dc:creator: Quentin Thomas, Clara Mefo Sop, Maxime Lavaud, Yacine Amarouchene, Thomas Salez, Pascal Damman

item.title: Tunable Signal Penetration and Response Plateaus in Bistable Mechanical Media
item.description: arXiv:2607.12405v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dynamic processing of mechanical signals is crucial for soft robotics and mechanosensing, yet classical viscoelastic materials lack intrinsic tunability and quantitative design rules. We show that internal bistability provides a simple but powerful mechanism to tailor response and signal attenuation in mechanical (meta)materials. In our model, bistable elements switch discretely with an intrinsic timescale between states that differ in potential energy $\epsilon$, equilibrium length $\Delta l$, and spring constant $\Delta k$. We combine Brownian dynamics simulations with discrete Poisson switching at rate $\nu$ and a nonlinear continuum (field) theory for the macroscopic strain relaxation. The model yields closed-form solutions for the linear response and the spatial penetration depth, revealing two complementary phenomena: a universal screening mechanism (akin to the electrostatic `skin effect') that strongly reduces signal penetration when the driving frequency exceeds the internal relaxation rate, and a frequency-insensitive response plateau arising from timescale separation. The attenuation strength, expressed by a screening length, is controlled primarily by the conformational length change $\Delta l$, while the attenuation regime and plateau position are tuneable via $\nu$. A parameter study exposes a fundamental design trade-off: larger $\Delta l$ strengthen dissipation but also raise the elastic energy barrier for state transitions, eventually causing state-locking where damping vanishes. Optimal attenuation thus emerges from a compromise between pronounced bistability and a surmountable barrier. Owing to its analytical tractability and generic formulation, our framework yields explicit design rules applicable to systems from biopolymers to synthetic catch bonds and metamaterials, enabling the design of soft materials with frequency-selective mechanical response.
item.dc:creator: Sven Pattloch, Joachim Dzubiella

item.title: A numerical study to analyze the interplay of Weissenberg number and viscosity ratio in a log-strain tensorial model for viscoelastic fluids
item.description: arXiv:2608.01925v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a computational study aimed at exploring the different and independent roles of the Weissenberg number and of the ratio between the polymeric and solvent viscosity contributions in a viscoelastic fluid model. The tensorial model under investigation, recently proposed, is based on a logarithmic relation between the elastic (or recoverable) strain and the elastic stress. In this model, the elastic strain plays the role of a conformation tensor and its evolution equation inherently preserves its determinant and positive definiteness. These properties are also enforced in the computational method employed in the study. A finite-difference discretization in time is combined with a stabilized mixed finite element formulation based on the Variational Multiscale method for the spatial discretization and with a generalized Lie derivative approach for the advection terms. The behavior of the model is analyzed in paradigmatic pressure-driven flows and we find that the value of the viscosity ratio is crucial in determining to which extent non-Newtonian flow profiles are observed upon increasing the Weissenberg number. By comparing the solutions of the log-strain tensorial model with those of a suitable Generalized Newtonian Fluid model, we show that flow-type dependence and memory play a significant role even in the simple planar flow past a cylinder.
item.dc:creator: Nehal Dash, Ramon Codina, Giulio G. Giusteri

item.title: Liquid-liquid phase transitions in dipolar liquids. Insights into Supercooled Water
item.description: arXiv:2609.02666v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dipolar liquids combine two coupled degrees of freedom, translational and dipolar. Intriguingly, these two sectors can reside in distinct thermodynamic states, with the state of one sector possibly favouring a specific state of the other. The onset of ferroelectric order in dipolar liquids is an example of this mutual stabilization. Since this coupling is often encoded in interaction potentials, projecting out one sector to derive an effective interaction for the other can uncover the microscopic mechanism underlying this phenomenon. A coarse-grained theory, solved in the large-dimensional limit, in which the distance between nearest-neighbour particles depends on their dipolar interaction through a density-dependent mechanical compliance shows that a ferroelectric transition can trigger a liquid-liquid transition. It also predicts a first-order liquid-liquid transition within the paraelectric phase that, in turn, can promote ferroelectric ordering. The anisotropic dipolar-dependent soft-core interaction is shown to lead to an effective Jagla-like isotropic two-length-scale interaction, known to support liquid-liquid phase transitions. Here, however, the two-length-scale pattern depends on density and dipolar configuration, and is therefore sensitive to dipolar order. Analysis of supercooled TIP4P/Ice water molecular dynamics simulations shows that first-coordination-shell features of the pair correlation functions are sensitive to dipolar interaction, supporting the foundations of the coarse-grained theory. Comparison of low- and high-density liquid water reveals enhanced spatial anisotropy of the first coordination shell in the low-density liquid, associated, within the theory, with increased effective excluded volume, showing that the liquid-liquid transition involves structural changes within the first shell, beyond reorganization of the interstitial region and tetrahedral order.
item.dc:creator: Maria Grazia Izzo

item.title: The effect of limb kinematics on the speed of a legged robot on granular media
item.description: arXiv:1303.7276v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Achieving effective locomotion on diverse terrestrial substrates can require subtle changes of limb kinematics. Biologically inspired legged robots (physical models of organisms) have shown impressive mobility on hard ground but suffer performance loss on unconsolidated granular materials like sand. Because comprehensive limb-ground interaction models are lacking, optimal gaits on complex yielding terrain have been determined empirically. To develop predictive models for legged devices and to provide hypotheses for biological locomotors, we systematically study the performance of SandBot, a small legged robot, on granular media as a function of gait parameters. High performance occurs only in a small region of parameter space. A previously introduced kinematic model of the robot combined with a new anisotropic granular penetration force law predicts the speed. Performance on granular media is maximized when gait parameters minimize body acceleration and limb interference, and utilize solidification features of granular media.
item.dc:creator: Chen Li, Paul B. Umbanhowar, Haldun Komsuoglu, Daniel I. Goldman

item.title: Thermodynamic Approach to Momentum Transport in Dense Fluids
item.description: arXiv:2606.10858v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a new framework for extending Chapman-Enskog theory beyond the hard-sphere fluid model. Rather than relying on effective hard sphere diameters, the approach makes use of on an exchange function which can be related to the thermodynamic properties of the system. We show that two existing extensions, including modified Enskog theory (MET), fit into this new framework. Based on our approach, we propose an alternative to MET that takes into account the potential interaction energy associated with the inter-particle interactions in the fluid. The proposed expression is applied to predicting the shear viscosity of several different simulated fluid models across a wide set of densities $0.05 \leq \rho^* \leq 0.8$ and temperatures $1.5 \leq T^* \leq 4.0$ in Lennard-Jones units. The fluid models considered include both the Weeks-Chandler-Anderson (WCA) fluid and the Lennard-Jones (LJ) fluid. At low and intermediate density, here taken to be $\rho^* \leq 0.3$, we report mean relative prediction errors between $2\%$ and $4\%$ for both these. Across all densities considered, the largest mean relative errors reported are $4.4\%$ and $8.1\%$ for the WCA fluid and LJ fluid respectively. We also investigate other interaction models, including a diatomic molecular model, in order to better understand the limitations of our approach.
item.dc:creator: Christopher Devik Fjeldstad, Jonas Bueie, Astrid S. de Wijn
